headline: He shot the Bend gunman. He's sorry for the four.
summary: Kaylub Giamanco, 36, whose daughters attend Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, killed the 16-year-old who attacked the school on October 15. Three boys, aged 5, 8 and 11, and a teacher were already dead. In his first interview, with Oregon Public Broadcasting, he said he lies awake: "I see faces, I hear voices, I hear screams."

cover_question.q: Did he do the right thing?

cover_answer: Police say he saved lives. He says the price is his sleep.
table_question: Can you do the right thing and still feel terrible about it?

5-7.script: A dad in Oregon stopped a person who was hurting people at a school. The police say he saved a lot of children, and a teacher helped by holding on to the person first. He feels sad as well as brave, like being happy and tired at once after a long day out. At your school the grown-ups have a plan. That is their job, not yours.
5-7.why: Brave and sad in one person. The long day makes it concrete.
5-7.why_long: A child this age takes one vivid detail for the whole and reads your face before your words, so the script never gives them the shotgun or the classroom, only a tired kid after a long day and the grown-ups at their own school. Shielded: only if they heard it first. Expect "could that happen at my school?" The grown-ups train for it.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: A 16-year-old shot his way into Silver Rail Elementary. A teacher threw her phone at him and tackled him. A father passing the school, Kaylub Giamanco, called 911, went in, and shot him while she held on. Like a relay: she bought the seconds, he ran them. He says sorry to the families of the four who died first.
8-12.why: Shots, a tackle, a call, a shot, an apology. One chain.
8-12.why_long: At this age a child builds chains of cause and effect, so the script gives the chain in order: the gunman, the teacher's tackle, the 911 call, the shot. The relay is a mechanism they run on sports day, and it keeps the teacher in the picture. Expect "why does he feel bad if he won?" Because he counts the four he was too late for.

13-17.script: Did he do the right thing? Kaylub Giamanco followed a 16-year-old with a shotgun into his daughters' school and shot him, then twice more as he reached for it. Police say he and an unarmed teacher saved lives. Second: he can't sleep. The price of doing right, or proof something failed earlier?
13-17.why: He saved children and can't sleep. The gun question is theirs.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: this man saved children, and he lies awake seeing faces. The script asks them to hold both, then puts the harder question straight, because they will meet it online anyway. Kuhn's point: arguing is a skill, and it improves against someone honest. Expect "so, for or against?" Answer honestly.

5-7.q: Why is he sad if he helped?
5-7.a: Some people were hurt before he got there, and he wishes he had been faster. Helping and sad can happen together.

8-12.q: Why did he go in instead of waiting?
8-12.a: He told 911 people would die, then went in. Police say he saved lives.
Three boys and a teacher died before he reached the room. He counts them.

13-17.q: Did he do the right thing?
13-17.a: Police say yes: he and the teacher saved lives. He calls it a weight.

13-17.q: Does this mean more guns in schools?
13-17.a: One case. An unarmed teacher tackled him first. Hold both.
